body.text: In short:
Solomon Islands is ending its controversial security pact with China.
The pact became a talking point of the Australian 2022 federal election and a symbol of China's ambitions in the region.
What's next?
Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale is set to sign a treaty with Australia on Wednesday.
Solomon Islands has told China it is scrapping its controversial 2022 security pact, as the Pacific Island nation prepares to sign a sweeping treaty with Australia.

The move, described by one analyst as a "massive win" for Australia, comes as Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale landed in Canberra on Tuesday afternoon ahead of a signing ceremony for the new treaty on Wednesday.

Mr Wale, who came to power in May, had already flagged that his government would "review" the contentious 2022 pact, which allows China to rotate its police training teams in Solomon Islands, with about two dozen permanent Chinese police in the country at one time.
On Tuesday afternoon, Nine Newspapers reported that Solomon Islands had "recently" informed China it would pull out of the pact.

The ABC has now confirmed through sources that Mr Wale's government informed Beijing that it will not renew the security agreement when it comes to the end of its five-year duration in April next year.
The ABC has contacted the Solomon Islands government, the Chinese Embassy in Solomon Islands and the Australian government for comment.
China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said China had "always developed its relations with Solomon Islands on the principle of equality".

"In its cooperation with Pacific Island countries, including Solomon Islands, China does not engage in geopolitical contest or bloc confrontation, and its cooperation is neither aimed at nor influenced by any third party.

"The international community should work together to help Pacific Island countries achieve sustainable development, putting their independent development first. Cooperation should be open and inclusive and should not target any third party."
'Massive win' for Australia
Foreign Minister Penny Wong called the 2022 agreement, inked during the Morrison government's tenure, Australia's "worst foreign policy blunder in the Pacific since the end of World War II".
Australia has long feared China was using policing to gain a security foothold in the Pacific, and the Albanese government has said it is in a "permanent contest" with China in the region.
In her major foreign policy address to the Senate on Tuesday. Foreign Minister Penny Wong said Australia had since offered "reliability and credibility" to Pacific partners.
"We have offered partnership that is enduring, that is practical, that is respectful, that strengthens Pacific regionalism to answer the region's challenges," she said.
Lowy Institute Pacific Islands program director Oliver Nobetau described news of the scrapping of the China-Solomon Islands deal as a "massive win" for Australia.
"Getting Solomon Islands to turn their backs on China has been the holy grail of all the Pacific engagement under the Albanese government,"
Mr Nobetau said.
"But it begs the question: what has Australia offered to Matthew Wale to backtrack on this? Has Australia offered something really significant here that we're not aware of?
"I think there must be a very big carrot on offer."

Earlier this month, the ABC reported Australian government budget assistance money meant for cyclone recovery and fuel shock assistance had been filtered into the accounts of Solomon Islands government MPs for special grants, known as constituency development funds.
Mr Wale is in Canberra, bringing with him a 24-strong delegation on a special chartered flight from Honiara — paid for by the Australian government — ahead of Wednesday's signing of the treaty.

The exact details of the treaty have not yet been officially released, but the ABC confirmed last month that the High Commissioner sent texts conveying that Australia will funnel $980 million in additional funding into the Pacific nation.

Leaked texts accessed by the ABC revealed $142 million would be allocated for Mr Wale's signature "free education" policy and $47.8 million to provide "visa improvements" and deal with "security requests from Solomon Islands".

Anna Powles, an associate professor in security studies at Massey University, who shared photographs in 2022 on social media of a leaked draft of the China-Solomon Islands security deal, said the move was "significant" and could potentially move the whole region in a different direction.
"It sends a strong signal about Solomon Islands foreign policy alignment under Matthew Wale and it ties Solomon Islands closer to Australia," she said.

On Monday, Solomon Islands Opposition Leader and former prime minister Manasseh Sogavare — the main architect of the 2022 agreement with China — said he believed Mr Wale was preparing to ditch the pact, which he warned could undermine ties with China.
"The country must carefully consider what it stands to lose from such a decision," he said on Monday.
Mr Nobateu warned that Mr Wale, who has already faced one motion of no confidence, was likely to face challenges in Honiara.
"He will have to be very confident that he can stay in power by doing this," he said.
"He's picking a side here, and for Australia, it's good. But it could lead to another challenge."
